title: Colleagues
hookLine: the Sigalovada's duties between workers and employers (DN 31)
tomorrow: how do you stop carrying work home every night?

cards: Some workplaces call themselves a family, and some bosses act as if that means you owe them your weekends. The Sigalovada Sutta has a clearer answer.
A young man named Sigala bows to the six directions every morning, because his father told him to. The Buddha meets him and gives the old ritual a new meaning: each direction is a relationship.
Parents, teachers, family, friends, spiritual guides. And below, the Buddha says, are workers and servants. So what does a boss owe you, and what do you owe back?
The sutta's answer is a list, and it runs both ways.

teach.b: Here's the list. An employer looks after workers in five ways: work suited to their strength; food and wages; care when they're sick; a share of special treats; and time off at the right times.
And workers, looked after like that, give back: they start before the employer and finish after, take only what's given, do their work well, and speak well of the employer. Notice the shape.
Not a ladder where care only flows up. A loop. Work matched to strength sounds a lot like not burning people out.
Time off at the right times sounds a lot like a weekend. And doing the work well and speaking well of the place: that's what a good colleague returns. Be honest about the setting, too.

This is an ancient household with servants, and some lines, like starting before the master, belong to that world. What carries over is the loop. Each side has duties, and each side's care makes the other's easier.
Colleagues, in the sutta's sense, aren't a family, and they aren't strangers.
They're people bound by duties both ways.

how: The Sigalovada Sutta is taught in Theravada communities as a code of conduct for lay people, and its duties between employers and workers are read as guidance for workplaces today.

o: people you must treat like your own family
people bound by duties running both ways
rivals competing for the boss's attention

games.q: the loop at work — tap the pairs.
p: time off at the right times
bowed to six directions each morning

s: in the Sigalovada, duties only run from workers up to the boss
employers owe five things too: fair work, wages, care in sickness, treats, time off.
the sutta says employers should care for workers when they're sick
it's one of the employer's five duties.
the Buddha told Sigala to stop bowing to the directions
he gave the bowing a new meaning: each direction is a relationship.

games.q: your manager covered your shift when you were sick. now a coworker is trashing her in the break room. what fits duties both ways?
o: speak well of her, honestly; that's part of what workers give back.
join in; complaining together is how coworkers bond.
stay out of it; duties at work are only about the tasks.
games.why: in the sutta, workers return care by doing good work and speaking well of the employer. a loop, not a ladder.

practice: Bring to mind one person you work or study alongside. Pick one duty from the list that fits: take a task that suits your strength, share something good, or speak well of them somewhere they'll never hear it.
Choose when you'll do it, and see yourself doing it.

wordCard.voice: Colleagues: people bound by duties both ways, care from those in charge, and good work and good words returned.

orig.note: Pali: kammakara, a worker; DN 31 places servants and workers in the lower direction.

carryVoice: Keep this one: duties both ways, a loop and not a ladder. Five of fifty.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (the six directions; the master's five duties to servants and workers and their five in return)
